abstract: News feeds are digitally available all around us, yet the cognitive mechanisms by which we decide what to spend time on, and what to skip, are not well understood. We formulate digital news consumption as an information foraging problem. In this formulation, users move between news articles, formalized as information patches, exploited them like agents consuming food in a canonical patch foraging task. The switching time between news article can be seen as a navigational process that happens at a time akin to the travel time in the canonical patch foraging formalism. To unravel mechanisms determining news reading times, we fit an evidence-accumulation model separately to each of 2,820 readers of a Norwegian newspaper across 1.9 million reads. Reading times are described by accumulation from a variable starting point, in which readers arrive already partly informed. We also show that readers can be divided into two groups reflecting different behavioral patterns that we name: committed and conditional reflecting different distributions of the fitted evidence accumulation model parameters. Our study opens up the opportunity to study the detailed cognitive mechanisms underlying news consumption and our preliminary analysis show that our information foraging approach can be generalized to our types of digital media human interact with on a daily basis.
